gloss: To praise someone or something publicly and enthusiastically.
examples: Critics *acclaimed* the young pianist after her first concert.
Readers still *acclaim* him as the finest writer of his generation.
Her second novel has been widely *acclaimed*.
contrast: Most often used in the passive: *a widely acclaimed writer*.

gloss: To make someone familiar with a person, a place, or a set of facts.
examples: Let me *acquaint* you with the house rules.
The tour *acquainted* us with the whole neighborhood.
They got *acquainted* at a wedding last summer.
contrast: Nearly always with *with*: *acquaint someone with something*, or *get acquainted with someone*.

gloss: To tell someone firmly but not angrily that they have done something wrong.
examples: Teachers often *admonish* students who talk during a test.
The judge *admonished* him for interrupting.
She has *admonished* the boys twice about their language.
contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: *admonishes*.

gloss: To annoy someone, or to make a bad situation worse.
examples: His constant humming *aggravates* everyone in the office.
She *aggravated* her sister by reading her messages.
He was *aggravating* the neighbors with loud music all weekend.
contrast: In American English it means both *annoy a person* and *make a problem worse* — the context decides which.

gloss: To give help or support to a person in need.
examples: Several charities *aid* families arriving in the city.
Neighbors *aided* them for weeks after the fire.
She has *aided* dozens of students with their applications.
contrast: *aid* is the verb; *aide* (same sound) is a noun meaning an assistant.

gloss: To make people stop being friendly toward you.
examples: Try not to *alienate* the people who can still help you.
His rudeness *alienated* half the family.
She is *alienating* the friends who supported her.

gloss: To make someone dislike you or become hostile toward you.
examples: Try not to *antagonize* your brother before the trip.
He *antagonized* the neighbors by parking in their spot.
She has *antagonized* everyone on the committee.
contrast: American *antagonize*; British *antagonise*.

gloss: To calm an angry person by giving them what they want.
examples: He brought flowers to *appease* his wife.
The apology *appeased* her for about an hour.
They have been *appeasing* the angry neighbors all week.

transitivity: both — transitive (*assist* a colleague), intransitive (she *assisted* with the move)
gloss: To help someone, especially by doing part of their work.
examples: Could you *assist* me with these bags?
A nurse *assisted* the doctor during the exam.
He has *assisted* the family since their father died.
contrast: *assist someone with something*, or *assist in doing something* — not *assist to do*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*associate* one thing with another), intransitive (don't *associate* with them)
gloss: To spend time with a particular person or group.
examples: Her parents didn't want her to *associate* with that crowd.
He *associated* mainly with musicians in those years.
They have been *associating* with the same friends since college.
contrast: The verb ends in -ayt (uh-SOH-see-ayt); the noun and adjective end in -it (uh-SOH-see-it).

gloss: To keep away from a person or a situation on purpose.
examples: She *avoids* her ex at every party.
He *avoided* me for a week after the argument.
They have been *avoiding* each other since the wedding.
contrast: *avoid* takes the -ing form, never the infinitive: *avoid meeting him*, not *avoid to meet him*.

gloss: To keep asking someone for something until they are worn out.
examples: Don't *badger* your sister about the money.
Reporters *badgered* him with questions for an hour.
She has been *badgering* me all month to join her book club.

gloss: To say unkind things about someone behind their back (informal).
examples: Don't *badmouth* your coworkers in front of the boss.
He *badmouthed* his old team in an interview.
She has been *badmouthing* me to all our friends.

gloss: To exchange light, friendly jokes with someone.
examples: The two cousins *banter* every time they meet.
They *bantered* about baseball for an hour.
He was *bantering* with the waitress while we waited.

transitivity: both — transitive (*beckon* the waiter), intransitive (she *beckoned* to me)
gloss: To signal someone to come toward you, usually with your hand.
examples: The doorman will *beckon* you when the car arrives.
She *beckoned* me over with one finger.
He stood at the gate, *beckoning* to the children.

gloss: To become a friend to someone, especially someone who needs one.
examples: Try to *befriend* the new neighbors.
An older student *befriended* him on his first day.
She has *befriended* every child on the block.
contrast: *befriend* takes a direct object: *befriend someone*, never *befriend with someone*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*behave* yourself), intransitive (he *behaves* badly in public)
gloss: To act in a particular way toward other people.
examples: *Behave* yourself while I'm gone.
The kids *behaved* beautifully at the restaurant.
He has been *behaving* strangely since the argument.
contrast: With no object it means *act well*: *the children behaved* = they were good.

gloss: To make a person or their achievements seem small or unimportant.
examples: Don't *belittle* what she has accomplished.
He *belittled* his wife in front of the guests.
She felt *belittled* by his comment about her job.

gloss: To scold someone loudly and at length.
examples: Never *berate* a child in public.
The coach *berated* the team at halftime.
He has been *berating* the staff all morning.

gloss: To tell a secret that you were supposed to keep (informal).
examples: Don't *blab* about the surprise party.
Someone *blabbed* to her mother.
He has been *blabbing* our news all week.
contrast: The single b doubles: *blab → blabbed → blabbing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the trip *bonded* the group), intransitive (they *bonded* quickly)
gloss: To form a close personal connection with someone.
examples: New parents often *bond* with other new parents.
The two men *bonded* over their love of fishing.
The team has *bonded* since the coach changed.
contrast: *bond with someone* — the preposition is almost always *with*.

gloss: To annoy someone, especially by not leaving them alone (informal).
examples: Stop *bugging* me about the car.
His whistling *bugged* everyone on the bus.
It has *bugged* me for years that she never called back.
contrast: The single g doubles: *bug → bugged → bugging*.

gloss: To touch someone gently and lovingly.
examples: She *caresses* his hand whenever he is nervous.
He *caressed* her cheek and said good night.
She sat *caressing* the baby's hair until he slept.
contrast: Two s's, and the third person adds -es: *caresses*.

gloss: To go with young people to an event in order to watch over them.
examples: Would you *chaperone* the field trip on Friday?
Two teachers *chaperoned* the school dance.
She has *chaperoned* every trip this year.
contrast: Also spelled *chaperon*; the ch sounds like sh.

gloss: To criticize someone sharply for something they have done.
examples: Parents sometimes *chastise* their children in public.
The principal *chastised* the students for the prank.
He was *chastised* in the press for his remarks.

transitivity: both — transitive (*coach* a team), intransitive (he *coaches* at the high school)
gloss: To train or guide a person, teaching them how to do something better.
examples: She *coaches* her daughter's soccer team.
He *coached* me through my first job interview.
They have been *coaching* together for ten years.
contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: *coaches*.

gloss: To gently persuade someone to do something they are unwilling to do.
examples: It took an hour to *coax* an apology out of him.
She *coaxed* her shy brother into dancing.
They were *coaxing* Grandma to stay another night.
contrast: Ends in -x, so the third person adds -es: *coaxes*.

gloss: To treat someone too gently and protect them from every difficulty.
examples: Don't *coddle* the kids so much.
His parents *coddled* him well into his twenties.
She has been *coddling* her students all semester.

gloss: To live near or with other people without fighting.
examples: The two families *coexist* peacefully on the same street.
For years the groups *coexisted* without trouble.
They have *coexisted* in one apartment since March.
contrast: The -x- here sounds like gz: koh-ig-ZIST.

gloss: To praise someone formally for something they have done well.
examples: I *commend* you on how you handled that.
The mayor *commended* the firefighters for their courage.
She has been *commended* twice for her volunteer work.
contrast: *commend* means praise; *recommend* means advise. Only *recommend* has the re-.

gloss: To accept behavior that most people think is wrong.
examples: The school does not *condone* bullying.
She *condoned* his rudeness for years.
By saying nothing, he has *condoned* their behavior.

transitivity: both — transitive (*confide* a secret), intransitive (*confide* in a friend)
gloss: To tell someone private things because you trust them.
examples: He *confides* only in his oldest friend.
She *confided* in her sister about the divorce.
I have never *confided* that to anyone.
contrast: You *confide in* a person, but you *confide* a secret *to* someone.

gloss: To come together in a group in one place.
examples: Students *congregate* in the hallway between classes.
A crowd *congregated* outside the church.
People were *congregating* near the entrance.

gloss: To have a conversation with someone.
examples: He can *converse* in three languages.
They *conversed* quietly in the corner all evening.
The two were *conversing* like old friends.
contrast: The verb is kuhn-VURS; the noun *converse* (the opposite) is KAHN-vurs.

gloss: To try to win someone's love or support over a period of time.
examples: Companies *court* students at job fairs.
He *courted* her for two years before proposing.
The candidate is *courting* younger voters.

transitivity: both — transitive (*cuddle* the baby), intransitive (they *cuddled* on the couch)
gloss: To hold someone close in your arms to show affection.
examples: They like to *cuddle* on the couch and watch movies.
She *cuddled* the baby until he fell asleep.
The kids were *cuddling* under one blanket.

gloss: To have earned something by what you are or what you have done.
examples: She *deserves* a better friend than him.
He *deserved* that apology and never got it.
They have *deserved* every bit of their good luck.
contrast: A state verb: say *he deserves it*, not *he is deserving it*.

gloss: To consider someone or something beneath your attention.
examples: He *disdains* small talk at parties.
She *disdained* their offer of help.
They have always *disdained* people who brag.

gloss: To try to stop someone from doing something, or to take away their confidence.
examples: Don't let one rude comment *discourage* you.
Her parents *discouraged* her from marrying so young.
The long wait has *discouraged* a lot of visitors.
contrast: *discourage someone from doing something* — the preposition is *from*, followed by -ing.

gloss: To bring shame on a person or a family.
examples: She refused to *disgrace* her parents' name.
He *disgraced* the family with his behavior at the wedding.
The former mayor has been *disgraced* by the scandal.

gloss: To say publicly that you no longer consider someone part of your family.
examples: Her father threatened to *disown* her.
They *disowned* their son after the trial.
He has been *disowned* by the whole family.

gloss: To treat someone rudely, as if they did not deserve respect.
examples: Don't *disrespect* your grandmother like that.
He felt she had *disrespected* him in front of his friends.
You are *disrespecting* everyone who worked on this.

gloss: To feel that someone cannot be trusted.
examples: She *distrusts* anyone who talks too much.
He *distrusted* his new neighbors from the start.
Voters have *distrusted* him since the scandal.

gloss: To leave a person you are with, suddenly and without warning (informal).
examples: Don't *ditch* your friends for a new boyfriend.
She *ditched* us at the mall and went home.
He has been *ditching* class to see her.
contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: *ditches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*dominate* the conversation), intransitive (one voice always *dominates*)
gloss: To control a person or a group, or to take up most of the attention.
examples: One family *dominates* the town's politics.
Her older brother *dominated* every conversation.
He has been *dominating* the group since he joined.

gloss: To love someone so much that you give them constant attention.
examples: Grandparents *dote* on a first grandchild.
She *doted* on her little brother.
He has always *doted* on his wife.
contrast: Always with *on* or *upon*: *dote on someone*.

gloss: To run away with someone in order to marry quietly, without a big wedding.
examples: Some couples *elope* to save money.
They *eloped* to Las Vegas last spring.
By the time we heard, they had already *eloped*.

gloss: To meet someone unexpectedly, or to run into a difficulty.
examples: You may *encounter* some resistance from his family.
We *encountered* an old classmate at the airport.
She has *encountered* the same rudeness before.

gloss: To make someone liked by other people.
examples: Complaining about the food will not *endear* you to your hosts.
She *endeared* herself to the neighbors by shoveling their walks.
That habit has not *endeared* him to his in-laws.
contrast: Almost always *endear yourself to someone* or *endear someone to someone*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*engage* a shy guest), intransitive (*engage* with the neighbors)
gloss: To draw someone into conversation or activity with you.
examples: She knows how to *engage* shy people in conversation.
They got *engaged* on New Year's Eve.
He has been *engaging* with the neighbors more since he retired.
contrast: *get engaged to someone* = обручиться; *engage with someone* = общаться. The silent -e drops: *engaging*.

gloss: To cause people who were close to become distant from each other.
examples: Money can *estrange* even the closest friends.
The argument *estranged* him from his brother.
She has been *estranged* from her father for years.
contrast: Usually in the participle: *his estranged wife*, *estranged from her family*.

gloss: To deliberately keep someone out of a group or an activity.
examples: Please don't *exclude* the younger kids.
They *excluded* him from the group chat.
She has felt *excluded* ever since the move.
contrast: *exclude someone from something* — the preposition is *from*.

gloss: To use a person unfairly for your own benefit.
examples: Some employers *exploit* workers who are new to the country.
He *exploited* his sister's kindness for years.
She felt *exploited* by her so-called friends.
contrast: The verb is ik-SPLOYT; the noun *exploit* (a brave deed) is EK-sployt.

gloss: To treat one person better than others, or to prefer one option.
examples: Their mother clearly *favors* the youngest.
The judges *favored* the local team.
He has always *favored* his oldest friends.
contrast: American *favor, favored, favoring*; British *favour, favoured, favouring*.

gloss: To carry on a long, bitter quarrel with another person or family.
examples: They *feud* over everything, even parking spots.
The two families *feuded* for three generations.
The brothers were *feuding* again at Thanksgiving.

gloss: To behave playfully toward someone to show you find them attractive.
examples: He *flirts* with everyone at the office.
She *flirted* with him all evening.
They were *flirting* by the coffee machine.
contrast: *flirt with someone* — never takes a direct object.

transitivity: both — transitive (*fool* your friends), intransitive (stop *fooling* and sit down)
gloss: To trick someone into believing something that is not true.
examples: You can't *fool* your own mother.
He *fooled* us all with that story about his uncle.
She has been *fooling* people for years.

gloss: To raise a child who is not your own for a period of time, or to encourage a feeling to grow.
examples: She wants to *foster* a teenager next year.
They *fostered* three children before adopting one.
The couple has been *fostering* since 2019.

gloss: To give someone a lot of anxious attention, or to worry aloud about small things.
examples: Grandma always *fusses* over the grandchildren.
He *fussed* about the seating chart all night.
Stop *fussing* — the guests won't notice.
contrast: *fuss over someone* = хлопотать вокруг; *fuss about something* = ворчать из-за. Third person adds -es: *fusses*.

gloss: To smile very widely, showing your teeth.
examples: She *grins* every time he tells that joke.
He *grinned* when he saw her at the door.
They stood there *grinning* at each other.
contrast: The single n doubles: *grin → grinned → grinning*.

gloss: To punish a child by not letting them go out with friends.
examples: If you lie to me again, I will *ground* you.
His parents *grounded* him for two weeks.
She has been *grounded* since the party.
contrast: This verb is regular — *grounded*. The identical form *ground* is also the past of the different verb *grind*.

gloss: To apologize or beg in a way that shows too much humility.
examples: You don't have to *grovel* — just apologize.
He *groveled* for a week before she forgave him.
She was still *groveling* the next morning.
contrast: American *groveled, groveling* (one l); British *grovelled, grovelling*.

gloss: To bother someone repeatedly with demands or questions (informal).
examples: Quit *hassling* your sister.
The kids *hassled* him for ice cream all afternoon.
Security has *hassled* him twice about his badge.

gloss: To interrupt a speaker or performer with rude shouts.
examples: Fans *heckle* the visiting team every year.
Someone in the back *heckled* the comedian.
He was *heckling* the speaker until security came.

gloss: To do something for someone that makes things easier for them.
examples: Could you *help* me carry this upstairs?
Her neighbors *helped* her through a hard winter.
He has *helped* me more than anyone in this family.
contrast: In American English the *to* is usually dropped: *she helped me move*, rather than *helped me to move*.

gloss: To go along with what someone wants so they will not be upset.
examples: Just *humor* him and listen to the story again.
She *humored* her grandfather for an hour.
We have been *humoring* him all evening.
contrast: American *humor, humored*; British *humour, humoured*.

gloss: To admire someone so much that you see no faults in them.
examples: Kids *idolize* athletes they have never met.
He *idolized* his older brother.
She has *idolized* that singer since middle school.
contrast: American *idolize*; British *idolise*.

gloss: To make someone part of a group or an activity.
examples: Be sure to *include* the new kid in the game.
They *included* us in every family holiday.
She has *included* her stepson in all the plans.
contrast: *include someone in something* — the preposition is *in*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*indulge* the children), intransitive (*indulge* in gossip)
gloss: To let someone have whatever they want, or to allow yourself a pleasure.
examples: She *indulges* her nephews terribly.
He *indulged* in a long lunch with old friends.
They have been *indulging* the baby since day one.
contrast: *indulge someone* = потакать кому-л.; *indulge in something* = позволить себе что-л.

gloss: To involve yourself in someone else's affairs when you are not wanted.
examples: Her mother *interferes* in every decision they make.
He *interfered* once too often and lost a friend.
Work has been *interfering* with their marriage.
contrast: *interfere in* someone's business, but *interfere with* a plan or a relationship.

gloss: To come into a place or a situation where you are not welcome.
examples: I don't want to *intrude* on your evening.
Reporters *intruded* on the family's grief.
She felt he was *intruding* into her private life.
contrast: *intrude on* or *intrude upon* someone.

gloss: To annoy someone in a small but persistent way.
examples: His constant advice *irks* his brother.
It *irked* her that no one thanked her.
The noise has *irked* the neighbors for months.

gloss: To keep a person apart from other people.
examples: Don't *isolate* yourself from your friends.
Shyness *isolated* him all through high school.
She has been *isolating* herself since the breakup.

transitivity: both — transitive (the crowd *jeered* him), intransitive (they *jeered* at the referee)
gloss: To shout rude, mocking remarks at someone.
examples: Boys on the corner *jeer* at anyone in a suit.
The crowd *jeered* when he dropped the ball.
They were *jeering* at the visiting team all night.

transitivity: both — transitive (*kid* your brother), intransitive (I'm only *kidding*)
gloss: To say something as a joke, especially to tease someone (informal).
examples: Don't *kid* yourself — she isn't coming back.
He *kidded* his sister about her new haircut.
I was only *kidding*, and she knew it.
contrast: The single d doubles: *kid → kidded → kidding*.

ru: вмешиваться, лезть не в своё дело
gloss: To interfere in matters that are none of your business.
examples: His aunt *meddles* in everyone's marriage.
She *meddled* once and lost a friend.
Stop *meddling* in things that don't concern you.
contrast: *meddle in* someone's affairs. Sounds exactly like the noun *medal* (медаль).

gloss: To advise and guide a younger or less experienced person over time.
examples: He wants to *mentor* students from his old school.
She *mentored* three young engineers last year.
He has been *mentoring* her since she joined the firm.

transitivity: both — transitive (*mingle* the two groups), intransitive (she *mingled* with the guests)
gloss: To move around at a party talking to many different people.
examples: Try to *mingle* instead of standing by the door.
The host *mingled* with her guests all evening.
They were *mingling* near the bar when we arrived.
contrast: *mingle with someone* — the preposition is *with*.

gloss: To act badly, especially as a child does.
examples: If you *misbehave*, we go home.
The twins *misbehaved* at their cousin's wedding.
He has been *misbehaving* in class all week.

gloss: To treat a person cruelly or unfairly.
examples: No one should *mistreat* a guest.
They *mistreated* the old man for years.
She has been *mistreated* by everyone she trusted.

gloss: To have doubts about whether someone can be trusted.
examples: He *mistrusts* anyone who is too friendly too fast.
She *mistrusted* his sudden kindness.
They have *mistrusted* each other since the argument.
contrast: *mistrust* and *distrust* mean nearly the same thing; *distrust* is the more common of the two in American English.

transitivity: both — transitive (*nitpick* every sentence), intransitive (he *nitpicks* constantly)
gloss: To find fault with tiny details that do not matter.
examples: He *nitpicks* everything she cooks.
They *nitpicked* about the seating chart for an hour.
Stop *nitpicking* and enjoy the party.

transitivity: both — transitive (duty *obliges* us), intransitive (she asked, and he *obliged*)
gloss: To force someone by duty to do something, or to do a favor they asked for.
examples: Family ties *oblige* us to visit at least twice a year.
She asked for one more song, and the band *obliged*.
He felt *obliged* to invite his cousin.
contrast: *be obliged to do something* = быть обязанным сделать что-л.

gloss: To shut someone out of a group completely.
examples: Small towns sometimes *ostracize* anyone who is different.
The other girls *ostracized* her after the rumor spread.
No one wants to be *ostracized* by their own family.
contrast: American *ostracize*; British *ostracise*.

gloss: To treat someone with great care and comfort.
examples: He *pampers* his wife on her birthday.
They *pampered* their guests with breakfast in bed.
She has been *pampering* her sister all week.

transitivity: both — transitive (*parent* a teenager), intransitive (they *parent* very differently)
gloss: To raise a child and care for them as a mother or father.
examples: They *parent* very differently from their own parents.
She *parented* four children on her own.
*Parenting* two teenagers is exhausting.

transitivity: both — transitive (he *partnered* her in the dance), intransitive (*partner* with a charity)
gloss: To join with another person or group to do something together.
examples: Will you *partner* with me for the project?
The school *partnered* with a local library.
They have been *partnering* on charity events for years.
contrast: In its common modern use it takes *with*: *partner with someone*.

gloss: To enjoy yourself at a party, usually late into the night.
examples: He *parties* every weekend.
They *partied* until three in the morning.
We were *partying* on the roof when it started raining.
contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied (*parties, partied*), but the -ing form keeps the y: *partying*.

gloss: To speak to someone as if they were less intelligent than you.
examples: Don't *patronize* me — I have done this longer than you have.
He *patronized* everyone who asked a simple question.
She felt *patronized* by her younger colleagues.
contrast: American PAY-truh-nyz; British PAT-ruh-nyz. It also means *to be a regular customer of a business*.

gloss: To keep annoying someone with requests or questions.
examples: Stop *pestering* your brother.
The kids *pestered* him for a dog all summer.
She has *pestered* me about it every day this week.

gloss: To play a trick on someone for fun.
examples: They *prank* each other every April Fools' Day.
He *pranked* his roommate with a rubber spider.
She has been *pranking* her coworkers all week.

gloss: To ask about things that are private and none of your business.
examples: I don't mean to *pry*, but are you two still together?
She *pried* until he told her everything.
He is always *prying* into other people's business.
contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied (*pries, pried*), but the -ing keeps the y: *prying*.

gloss: To argue about small, unimportant details.
examples: Let's not *quibble* about ten dollars.
They *quibbled* over who would pay the check.
The cousins were still *quibbling* when we left.

gloss: To criticize someone sharply for what they have said or done.
examples: No one dared to *rebuke* the boss.
The coach publicly *rebuked* his star player.
He has been *rebuked* twice this month.

transitivity: both — transitive (*reciprocate* a kindness), intransitive (she never *reciprocated*)
gloss: To give back the same feeling or favor that someone gave you.
examples: They invited us to dinner, so we should *reciprocate*.
He loved her, but she never *reciprocated*.
She has *reciprocated* every kindness we showed her.

transitivity: both — transitive (he *remarried* his first wife), intransitive (she never *remarried*)
gloss: To marry again after a divorce or the death of a husband or wife.
examples: He says he will never *remarry*.
She *remarried* two years after the divorce.
Her mother has *remarried* twice.
contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied (*remarries, remarried*), but the -ing keeps the y: *remarrying*.

gloss: To talk with pleasure about things that happened long ago.
examples: They love to *reminisce* at family dinners.
The old friends *reminisced* about their college years.
We were *reminiscing* about our first apartment.
contrast: *reminisce about something*. The ending -sce sounds like -ss: rem-uh-NIS.

gloss: To tell someone officially that they have done something wrong.
examples: Managers rarely *reprimand* anyone in public.
The teacher *reprimanded* him in front of the class.
She was *reprimanded* for arriving late three days in a row.

gloss: To tell someone with sadness or disappointment that they have let you down.
examples: He has nothing to *reproach* himself for.
She *reproached* him for forgetting her birthday.
Her eyes were *reproaching* me the whole evening.
contrast: *reproach someone for something*. Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: *reproaches*.

gloss: To come together again after a long separation.
examples: The agency helps *reunite* families.
The sisters *reunited* after thirty years apart.
They have been *reunited* at last.

transitivity: both — transitive (*salute* an officer), intransitive (the soldiers *saluted*)
gloss: To greet someone respectfully, or to honor them publicly.
examples: He *salutes* his neighbor with a wave every morning.
The soldiers *saluted* as the general passed.
The town has *saluted* her for fifty years of service.

transitivity: both — transitive (*schmooze* the donors), intransitive (he *schmoozed* all night)
gloss: To chat in a friendly way with people who may be useful to you (informal).
examples: She knows how to *schmooze* a room full of strangers.
He *schmoozed* with everyone at the reception.
They were *schmoozing* with donors until midnight.

gloss: To reject or look down on someone with open contempt.
examples: They *scorn* anyone who leaves the neighborhood.
She *scorned* his apology and walked away.
He has been *scorned* by his old friends ever since.

gloss: To persuade someone into a romantic relationship, or into doing something unwise.
examples: He tried to *seduce* her with expensive gifts.
The idea of easy money *seduced* them both.
He was *seducing* half the town, or so the rumor went.

gloss: To deliberately keep away from a person or from company.
examples: She *shuns* parties and big crowds.
The whole village *shunned* him after the trial.
They have been *shunned* by their relatives for years.
contrast: The single n doubles: *shun → shunned → shunning*.

gloss: To tell someone in authority what another person did wrong (informal).
examples: Don't *snitch* on your own brother.
Someone *snitched* on us to the principal.
He has been *snitching* to the boss all year.
contrast: *snitch on someone*. Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: *snitches*.

gloss: To smile or speak in a way that shows contempt for someone.
examples: They *sneer* at anyone who tries hard.
He *sneered* at her homemade dress.
She was *sneering* the whole time I spoke.
contrast: *sneer at someone* — it takes no direct object.

gloss: To look secretly into someone's private things.
examples: Don't *snoop* around in my room.
She *snooped* through his phone while he slept.
He has been *snooping* on the neighbors again.

gloss: To ignore someone on purpose in a way that insults them.
examples: Don't *snub* your cousins just because they came late.
She *snubbed* him in front of everyone at the party.
He felt *snubbed* when they left him off the list.
contrast: The single b doubles: *snub → snubbed → snubbing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*snuggle* the baby close), intransitive (they *snuggled* under a blanket)
gloss: To settle close against someone for warmth and comfort.
examples: They like to *snuggle* under one blanket.
The children *snuggled* against their mother.
The puppy was *snuggling* into his lap.

transitivity: both — transitive (*socialize* a shy dog), intransitive (they rarely *socialize*)
gloss: To spend time with other people in a friendly way.
examples: They rarely *socialize* with the neighbors.
She *socialized* much more after she changed jobs.
He has been *socializing* a lot since the divorce.
contrast: American *socialize*; British *socialise*.

gloss: To quarrel noisily over something unimportant.
examples: Brothers *squabble*; that is normal.
The kids *squabbled* over the last piece of cake.
They were *squabbling* about money again.

gloss: To tell a parent or teacher what another child did wrong.
examples: Nobody likes a kid who *tattles*.
He *tattled* on his sister for staying up late.
She was *tattling* to the teacher every single day.
contrast: *tattle on someone* — the preposition is *on*.

gloss: To make someone want to do something, especially something they should not do.
examples: Don't *tempt* him with another drink.
The offer *tempted* her to leave the city.
I have been *tempted* to call her all week.

gloss: To worry someone, or to bother them with a request.
examples: Sorry to *trouble* you so late.
The news *troubled* the whole family.
Something has been *troubling* her for weeks.

gloss: To remove someone from your list of friends on a social network.
examples: Don't *unfriend* your own cousin over politics.
She *unfriended* him the day after the argument.
He has *unfriended* half his old classmates.

transitivity: both — transitive (*wave* your hand), intransitive (she *waved* from the car)
gloss: To move your hand in the air to greet someone or say goodbye.
examples: *Wave* goodbye to Grandma.
She *waved* to us from the train window.
He was *waving* his arms to get our attention.
contrast: The silent -e drops before -ing: *wave → waving*. You *wave to* or *wave at* a person.

gloss: To try to win someone's love, support, or business.
examples: Candidates *woo* voters with easy promises.
He *wooed* her with letters for a year.
The company has been *wooing* her since March.
contrast: Both o's stay in every form: *woo → wooed → wooing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*worship* a hero), intransitive (they *worship* on Sunday)
gloss: To love and admire someone so deeply that you treat them as perfect.
examples: She *worships* her older sister.
He *worshiped* his father when he was a boy.
They have *worshiped* at the same church for years.
contrast: American *worshiped, worshiping* (one p); British *worshipped, worshipping*.
